strengths: Well-motivated insight that temporal scaling is extrapolation rather than interpolation (Figure 1), challenging a common assumption in mixed-length video training
Technically sound methodology with clear formulation of gradient conflict between mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives, and principled use of DMD/VSD gradient surrogates
Dual-head architecture with shared encoder is an elegant solution to the gradient interference problem, with proper ablations demonstrating necessity of all components

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple quantitative metrics (VBench-Long + Gemini MLLM), strong baselines including recent AR methods (CausVid, Self-Forcing, InfinityRoPE), and convincing qualitative results
Clear presentation with good organization, insightful figures, and detailed technical descriptions of methodology and implementation
weaknesses: Critical evaluation-claim mismatch: paper claims minute-scale generation but only evaluates on 30-second videos; no quantitative results on actual 60+ second videos despite this being central to the contribution

Limited novelty in components: flow matching, reverse-KL distillation via DMD/VSD, and dual-head architecture are largely from prior work; primary contribution is their combination which is incremental
Heavy dependence on concurrent work (DDT by Wang et al. 2025c) for core architectural elements, raising reproducibility concerns and making it difficult to assess independent contribution
Modest quantitative improvements (mostly <1-2% gains in Table 1) with no statistical significance testing; some metrics show negligible differences (e.g., Motion 0.9548 vs 0.9541)
Data requirements still substantial (100k+ videos) despite framing around data scarcity, with significant portion from proprietary internet collection, limiting reproducibility and adoption
Insufficient analysis of method sensitivity: no thorough study of teacher quality impact, limited test set size (200 prompts), and no error analysis or failure case discussion
Potential evaluation bias: using Wan 1.3B model as both student and teacher; unclear how sensitive method is to teacher quality or domain mismatch
Limited discussion of computational costs (e.g., vfake score matching overhead) and practical deployment considerations

strengths: Clear motivation: Figure 1 effectively explains why temporal scaling differs from spatial resolution scaling, providing intuitive grounding for the approach
Well-motivated architecture: Decoupling mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives into separate heads is reasonable and supported by ablations (Table 2)
Practical efficiency: Achieves 4-step inference while maintaining quality, valuable for real-world deployment
Comprehensive presentation: Clear writing, good figures, thorough implementation details, and honest discussion of limitations
Proper ablation study: Table 2 demonstrates necessity of all major components (DDT design, sliding-window DMD, SFT supervision)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core components (DDT, DMD/VSD, Flow Matching) are from prior work; main contribution is straightforward application to sliding windows

Inconsistent empirical gains: Table 1 shows the method actually underperforms baselines on several key metrics (Motion: 0.9548 vs 0.9573 for InfinityRoPE; Subject Consistency: 0.9682 vs 0.9689; Background: 0.9548 vs 0.9614), with strong advantages only on subjective metrics like aesthetic quality

Evaluation at 30 seconds contradicts minute-scale claims: Despite claiming to solve minute-scale generation, testing uses only 30-second videos; no evaluation on 60+ second videos validates long-horizon capability

Unfair baseline comparisons: Compares against orthogonal AR methods (acknowledged by authors as such) and weak SFT baselines; missing comparisons with recent diffusion-based long-video methods (BlockVid, LongLive, etc.)

Insufficient technical analysis: Fake score estimator trained for only 5 steps without sensitivity analysis; gradient flow design (stop-gradient on v_fake - u_teacher) not justified; hyperparameter λ_seg not disclosed

Limited experimental scope: Same model (Wan 1.3B) as both teacher and student limits generalizability; only 200 test prompts; no user studies; no ablation on data scarcity despite claiming to learn from limited long videos
Reproducibility concerns: Code availability not mentioned; reliance on proprietary FastGen repository; key hyperparameter λ_seg not specified in main text
Missing critical ablations: No analysis of window length/stride sensitivity, λ_seg sensitivity, v_fake training duration impact, or computational overhead of sliding-window DMD

strengths: Novel problem insight: Identifies that temporal length requires extrapolation rather than interpolation, elegantly explaining mixed-length training failures
Well-motivated architecture: Gradient interference argument compelling; decoupling mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives through separate heads is principled solution
Thorough experimental validation: Comprehensive ablation study (Table 2), comparisons across multiple baseline classes, strong quantitative and qualitative results
Sound technical approach: Careful adaptation of DMD/VSD to sliding windows, proper handling of image/video latent boundary issues, clear training procedure
Practical improvements: Achieves 4-step fast inference while maintaining quality; requires no additional short-video data beyond frozen teacher
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations (Figure 1's extrapolation insight particularly compelling); accessible methodology description
weaknesses: Critical evaluation-claim mismatch: Abstract claims 'minute-scale' generation but evaluation limited to 30 seconds; no evidence at 60s, 90s, or true minute+ durations
Missing human evaluation: For generative models, perceptual quality and fidelity claims require human studies; reliance solely on automated metrics (VBench, Gemini) is insufficient
Reproducibility concerns: Uses proprietary/restricted datasets (Sekai, MiraData subsets); no clear path for reproduction; code release not mentioned; data statistics vague
Teacher dependence underexplored: All experiments use Wan 1.3B as student and teacher; no analysis of cross-model teachers, teacher quality impact, or behavior with weaker teachers
Limited technical novelty: Core components (DMD, DDT, FM/DM heads) from prior work; main contribution is engineering and problem framing rather than fundamental innovation
Incomplete ablations: No sensitivity analysis for critical hyperparameters (λ_seg weight, window size L, fake score steps); arbitrary choices (61s bound) unjustified
Evaluation limitations: Test set of 200 prompts modest for video generation; no failure case analysis or robustness studies; metric selection may bias toward proposed method
Metric reliability concerns: VBench consistency metrics acknowledged to favor static AR outputs; Gemini evaluation is post-hoc with single model; this undermines metric-based claims
Unfair computational comparisons: Comparing 4 NFE (ours) vs 50 NFE (baselines) conflates quality with computational budget; SFT baselines may be undertrained
Inference speed claims unsubstantiated: Claims 'fast few-step' but provides no wall-clock timing; 4 diffusion steps still requires multiple passes; comparison to real-time methods missing

strengths: Well-motivated fundamental insight about temporal extrapolation vs. spatial interpolation, clearly articulated with effective visualization
Rigorous mathematical motivation for gradient interference between mean-seeking and mode-seeking objectives, with clear justification for architectural decoupling
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple baseline categories, ablation studies, user studies (31 participants), and 60-second stress tests demonstrating robustness
Strong empirical results across multiple metrics (VLM Consistency 75.42, Dynamic Degree 0.9453) with competitive or superior performance relative to baselines
Practical solution addressing real architectural challenges (image-video latent mismatch via VAE re-encoding) and avoiding need for additional short-video training data
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (compositional instructions, entity memory) rather than overstating contribution scope
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: sliding-window reverse-KL is primarily adapted from existing DMD/VSD literature; main contribution (routing objectives to separate heads) is sensible but incremental
Circular dependency on concurrent work (Decoupled Diffusion Transformer by Wang et al., 2026b) predetermines architectural design, limiting attribution of contribution novelty

Evaluation scope misalignment: main results on 30-second videos (not truly 'minute-scale'); 60-second evaluation excludes SFT-only baselines for fair comparison, and VBench-Long metrics may not capture compositional reasoning or temporal causality

Significant reproducibility concerns: proprietary datasets (Sekai, MiraData) and base models (Wan 1.3B/14B), no code release, missing critical hyperparameters, dependency on specialized frameworks (DeepSpeed Ulysses, FastGen)

Under-justified design choices: lightweight head parameter overhead unexplored, full-range temporal attention scalability analysis missing, hyperparameter λ_seg not ablated, fake score estimator training procedure poorly specified
Inference efficiency claims unclear: NFE=4 matches teacher-only baselines; wall-clock speedup not compared; decomposition of speedup sources (steps vs. DM head) not separated
Missing dataset analysis: no sensitivity to long-video data proportion/amount, no scaling analysis to significantly longer sequences (5+ minutes), composition of long vs. short data unclarified
No gradient flow visualization demonstrating claimed gradient interference; limited analysis of FM vs. DM head-specific learning; failure case analysis only in supplementary material
Teacher quality dependency not analyzed; no study of robustness to suboptimal teachers or generalization to different teacher architectures
Unfair baseline comparisons: LongLive is frame-level AR real-time system (different class); acknowledged but critical failures (action state changes, entity revisitation) not quantitatively evaluated
